intro: Listen to a talk in a history class.
talk: So, here's a question that sounds silly at first: who decides what time it is? Before the 1880s, the answer in the United States was basically, the sun. Each town set its clocks by local solar time, so when it was noon in Chicago, it was already a few minutes past noon in towns to the east. For a farmer, that was fine. For a railroad, it was chaos. Each company ran on its own time, and a busy station might display several clocks at once. In fact, there were dozens of separate railroad times in use. Now, Britain had faced this problem earlier, in the 1840s, and its solution was simple: the railways adopted one national time, Greenwich time. But Britain is small. The United States spans about four hours of solar time, so a single national time wouldn't work. The solution the American railroads chose was zones. On November 18, 1883, they switched to four standard time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain, and Pacific. People called it the day of two noons, because in many towns the clocks struck twelve, were set back, and later struck twelve again. A year later, in 1884, an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the world's prime meridian. But here's what surprises students. Congress didn't make the time zones official until 1918. So for thirty-five years, the time most Americans lived by was set not by the government, but by private companies. The law simply caught up.

intro: Listen to a talk in a history class.
talk: Today let's look at what happened to ordinary workers after the Black Death. The plague reached England in 1348, and within about two years it had killed somewhere between a third and a half of the population. Think about that economically. Suddenly there were far fewer people to plow fields and bring in harvests, but the land was still there. So laborers were scarce, and scarce things get expensive. Workers began demanding higher wages, and many simply moved to whichever lord offered the best terms. Landowners didn't like this. So the government responded in two steps. First came an emergency ordinance in 1349, and then, in 1351, the Statute of Laborers, which tried to freeze wages at their pre-plague levels and made it illegal to refuse work. Did it work? Only partly. Wages still rose, and resentment over these controls, along with new taxes, fed into the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Over the following century, serfdom in England largely faded away. Now, historians used to tell this as a simple story: the plague made labor scarce, so peasants became free. But compare England with parts of Eastern Europe, like Poland and Prussia. There, labor was also scarce compared with the amount of land, yet over the next two centuries, lords actually tightened their control, binding peasants more firmly to their estates. Same kind of shortage, opposite result. So the current view is that the plague created pressure, but what happened next depended on who held power.

intro: Listen to a talk in an archaeology class.
talk: For most of the twentieth century, the textbook sequence went like this. First, people settled down and started farming. Then, with food surpluses, they had the time and the labor to build big monuments and temples. Farming first, monuments later. Göbekli Tepe, a hilltop site in southeastern Turkey, turned that sequence upside down. Excavations led by the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began in 1995, and his team uncovered large circular enclosures ringed by T-shaped limestone pillars. Some pillars are over five meters tall and weigh ten tons or more, and many are carved with animals: foxes, boars, snakes, vultures. The oldest enclosures date to around 9600 BCE. That's more than six thousand years before Stonehenge, and, crucially, before there's any clear evidence of domesticated crops or animals in the region. So who built it? Hunter-gatherers. Schmidt's interpretation was striking. He argued that Göbekli Tepe was a ceremonial center, a place where people gathered for rituals and feasts, but where nobody actually lived. He summed it up with a memorable phrase: first came the temple, then the city. Now, since Schmidt's death in 2014, newer excavations have complicated that picture. Archaeologists have found what look like houses, a system for collecting rainwater, and thousands of grinding stones for processing wild grain. So it now seems people did live at the site. The pillars are no less astonishing, but the neat contrast between a pure temple and an ordinary settlement has largely dissolved.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about archaeology.
talk: Welcome back. Today's object is a lump of corroded bronze that turned out to be one of the most surprising finds in archaeology. In 1900, sponge divers sheltering from a storm near the small Greek island of Antikythera spotted a shipwreck on the seabed. Divers brought up statues, pottery, and coins. The ship had sunk sometime around 70 to 60 BCE. Among the finds was a shoebox-sized wooden case, so badly decayed that nobody paid it much attention. Then, in 1902, an archaeologist noticed a gear wheel embedded in one of the fragments. A gear? From ancient Greece? Many scholars assumed it must come from a later period, or that it was a simple navigation instrument. In the 1950s, the historian Derek de Solla Price argued that it was a calculating device, and in the 1970s he used X-rays to count the gear teeth. Then, starting in 2005, researchers used high-resolution CT scanning, which revealed inscriptions hidden inside the fragments, basically a user's manual. Here's what we now know. Turning a handle drove at least thirty interlocking gears, and pointers showed the positions of the sun and moon, the phases of the moon, and the dates of eclipses. One dial even tracked the four-year cycle of athletic games, including the Olympics. That's why it's often called the first analog computer. And here's the strangest part: nothing with comparable gearing appears in the historical record for more than a thousand years, until the astronomical clocks of medieval Europe.

intro: Listen to a talk in an anthropology class.
talk: Today we're looking at a famous book in anthropology, and a famous argument about it. In 1925, a twenty-three-year-old Margaret Mead traveled to the island of Ta'ū in American Samoa. She spent about nine months there, observing and interviewing dozens of adolescent girls. Her question came from a debate back home. Many American psychologists claimed that adolescence was naturally a time of storm and stress, that the emotional turmoil of teenagers was biological. If that were true, Mead reasoned, it should happen everywhere. In her 1928 book, Coming of Age in Samoa, she reported that it didn't. Samoan girls, she wrote, passed through adolescence calmly, with relatively relaxed attitudes about relationships. So the turmoil of American teenagers had to be cultural, not biological. The book became a bestseller. Then, in 1983, five years after Mead died, the anthropologist Derek Freeman published a fierce critique. Freeman had worked in Samoa for years, and he argued that Samoan society actually placed a strong value on virginity and had plenty of conflict and violence. He even suggested that some of Mead's informants had been joking with her. So who was right? Well, most anthropologists today wouldn't simply side with Freeman, either. His fieldwork was done mostly in a different part of Samoa, and decades later, after major social changes. What the controversy really exposed was a problem of method: how much can one researcher, working alone in one place for a few months, claim to know about an entire culture?

intro: Listen to a talk in an anthropology class.
talk: In 1958, the anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his wife arrived in a small village in Bali to do fieldwork. For about ten days, the villagers treated them as if they didn't exist. Then, one afternoon, the couple attended a cockfight, which was illegal at the time. The police raided it, and everyone ran, including the two anthropologists, who fled alongside the villagers and hid in a courtyard. The next day, the whole village suddenly accepted them. From that fieldwork came his famous 1972 essay, 'Deep Play.' Geertz borrowed two ideas to make sense of the cockfight. The first was thick description, a phrase from the philosopher Gilbert Ryle. Ryle's example was two boys rapidly contracting their right eyelids. For one, it's an involuntary twitch; for the other, it's a wink, a signal to a friend. A camera records the same movement. Only a thick description, one that captures meaning, tells them apart. The second idea, deep play, came from Jeremy Bentham, who used it for bets so high that it's irrational to make them. Geertz noticed two kinds of betting. Side bets between individual spectators were mostly about money. But the large central bet, pooled by groups of allies, was about status. The higher those stakes, the more the fight was really about honor. So, Geertz concluded, the cockfight was a story the Balinese told themselves about themselves. Critics later asked a pointed question, though: whose story? Geertz, they said, rarely asked the participants what they thought.

intro: Listen to a talk in an art history class.
talk: Today: a painter who changed how light works in pictures. Michelangelo Merisi, known as Caravaggio, was born in 1571 and died in 1610, before he turned forty. In that short career, he developed a style we call tenebrism, from the Italian word for darkness. Now, you've heard of chiaroscuro, the contrast of light and shadow. Painters had used it for a century. But compare Leonardo's approach with Caravaggio's. Leonardo blended light into shadow so gradually, so smoothly, that you can't see where one ends and the other begins. Caravaggio did the opposite. His figures emerge from almost black backgrounds, struck by a strong light from a single source, often outside the frame, like a spotlight in a dark room. A great example is The Calling of Saint Matthew, finished around 1600 for a chapel in Rome. Christ points across a dim room at a group of men counting money, and a beam of light follows his gesture. And Caravaggio painted saints as ordinary people, with dirty feet and wrinkled faces, using models from the street. He influenced a generation of followers, the Caravaggisti, across Europe. Now, for a long time it was said that Caravaggio never drew, that he painted straight onto the canvas without any preparation. After all, no drawings by him survive. But technical studies have found lines scratched into the wet ground layer of his canvases, marking where figures would go. So he did plan, just not on paper, the way other painters did.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about art history.
talk: Today's episode is about how a cheap kind of Japanese print ended up transforming European painting. For over two centuries, Japan had sharply limited contact with the West. Then, in 1854, under pressure from American warships, it signed a treaty opening its ports, and Japanese goods began flowing to Europe. Among them were ukiyo-e, woodblock prints showing actors, landscapes, and city life. Now, each print was a team effort. A designer drew the image. A carver cut it into wooden blocks, a separate block for each color. A printer pressed the paper onto the blocks, one after another. Then a publisher sold them cheaply, like posters. In Japan, these were popular entertainment, not high art. Parisian artists saw them as revelations. After Japan exhibited at the Paris World's Fair of 1867, the craze took off, and by 1872 a critic had a name for it: Japonisme. So what did Europeans take from the prints? Flat areas of bright color, bold outlines, unusual high viewpoints, and figures cut off by the edge of the frame. Compare two painters. Vincent van Gogh copied prints by Hiroshige almost directly, in oil, even painting Japanese characters into the borders. Edgar Degas did something subtler. He borrowed the compositions, the off-center figures and cropped edges, but his subjects stayed entirely Parisian: dancers, racehorses, cafés. And here's the irony. Just as Europe was celebrating these prints as fine art, Japan, eager to modernize, was treating them as disposable and old-fashioned.

intro: Listen to a talk in a music history class.
talk: Today: sonata form, the structure behind the first movements of most symphonies, sonatas, and string quartets from the classical period, roughly 1750 to 1820. The standard textbook version has three sections. First comes the exposition, which presents two main themes. The first theme is in the home key. Then a transition moves to a new key, usually the dominant, a fifth higher, and the second theme appears there, often more lyrical. The second section is the development. Here the composer breaks the themes into fragments, moves restlessly through different keys, and builds tension. The third section is the recapitulation, where both themes return, but now, crucially, the second theme stays in the home key. That's what resolves the tension. So: exposition, development, recapitulation. Easy to memorize. But here's what textbooks rarely stress. Haydn and Mozart never used the term sonata form. It was coined in the 1840s by theorists like Adolf Bernhard Marx, who described the form mainly in terms of contrasting themes. An earlier theorist, Heinrich Christoph Koch, writing in 1793, during Haydn's lifetime, described the same movements in terms of keys rather than themes: a journey away from home and back again. And Koch's view fits Haydn better. In many of Haydn's movements, the so-called second theme is just the first theme again, in the new key. By Marx's definition, those movements barely qualify. By Koch's, they fit perfectly. So sonata form was a description written after the fact, not a recipe composers followed.

intro: Listen to a talk in a music history class.
talk: Before public concerts, where did people hear music? Mostly in church, at noble courts, and in private homes. If you were a composer, you worked for a patron, a church or a prince, and you wrote what your employer needed. Then, in London in 1672, a violinist named John Banister did something new. He advertised in a newspaper that music would be performed every afternoon at his house, and anyone could attend for a shilling. That's often considered the first series of public concerts with paid admission. Now, compare this with Paris. There, public concerts developed differently. The most important series, the Concert Spirituel, founded in 1725, operated under a royal privilege, and it originally performed on religious holidays when the opera houses were closed. So in Paris, concert life grew under the protection of the crown, while in London it grew as a business. And by the late 1700s, the London market was strong enough for an impresario named Johann Peter Salomon to bring Joseph Haydn over, twice, in the 1790s. Haydn wrote twelve symphonies for those visits, and he wrote them for a paying public. You know the Surprise Symphony, with the sudden loud chord in the quiet slow movement? The famous story is that Haydn wanted to wake up sleeping listeners. He later denied that, saying he simply wanted to do something new and make a brilliant debut. Either way, notice who he was trying to impress: not a prince, but a ticket-buying crowd.

intro: Listen to a talk in an architecture class.
talk: Let's talk about the Pantheon in Rome, perhaps the most impressive dome ever built. The building we see today was completed under the emperor Hadrian, around 125 CE, although the inscription on the front credits Agrippa, who built an earlier temple on the site. Now, the numbers. The dome spans about forty-three meters, and the height from the floor to the top is exactly the same, so a perfect sphere would fit inside. At the top is the oculus, an open hole about eight meters across, with no glass. And here's the remarkable part: the dome is unreinforced concrete, no steel at all, and nearly nineteen hundred years later, it's still the largest dome of its kind in the world. So how did the Romans do it? Three strategies. First, they varied the aggregate, the stones mixed into the concrete. Near the base, they used heavy material like travertine; higher up, they switched to lighter volcanic stone, with pumice near the top. Second, the dome's thickness decreases from about six meters at the base to just over one meter at the oculus. Third, the coffers, the sunken ceiling panels, remove even more weight. Compare that with Brunelleschi's dome in Florence, finished in the 1430s. It's slightly wider, but it's built of brick, with two shells, inner and outer. For a long time, people talked about a lost Roman secret. But really, the key was ordinary volcanic ash, which helps concrete set strongly even in damp conditions.

intro: Listen to a talk in an architecture class.
talk: So, why did the skyscraper appear in Chicago in the 1880s? There were really three conditions. The first was a disaster. In 1871, the Great Chicago Fire destroyed much of the city's center, and during rebuilding, land in the business district became very expensive. The economic logic was simple: if land is costly, build up. The second condition was the safety elevator. Elisha Otis had demonstrated one in New York in 1854, with a brake that stopped the car if the cable broke. Without elevators, nobody wanted to climb past five or six floors. But the third condition was the real structural problem. In a traditional building, the walls carry the weight, and the taller you build, the thicker the walls at the bottom have to be. Look at the Monadnock Building in Chicago, completed in 1891. It's sixteen stories tall with load-bearing brick walls, and at the base those walls are about six feet thick. That's about the limit. Now compare the Home Insurance Building, designed by William Le Baron Jenney and completed in 1885. It used an internal metal frame to carry much of the load, so the walls could be thinner. It's usually called the first skyscraper, even though it was only ten stories. But historians argue about that title. Jenney's frame still relied partly on masonry, and others were experimenting too. So the skyscraper wasn't a single invention. It was a gradual shift from walls that hold a building up to a frame that does.

intro: Listen to a talk in a literature class.
talk: Today we're comparing two versions of the sonnet. Every sonnet has fourteen lines, but how those lines are organized changes how the poem thinks. Start with Petrarch, in fourteenth-century Italy. The Petrarchan sonnet divides into two parts: an octave of eight lines, then a sestet of six. The octave usually rhymes A-B-B-A, A-B-B-A, so it reuses just two rhyme sounds, four times each. And between the octave and the sestet, at line nine, there's a turn, which Italian critics call the volta. The octave raises a problem; the sestet answers or reconsiders it. Now, poets like Thomas Wyatt brought the sonnet to England in the 1530s. But there was a practical difficulty. Italian is full of words with similar endings, so rhymes are easy to find. English has far fewer rhyming words, and finding four rhymes on the same sound, twice, is hard. So English poets gradually developed a different structure: three quatrains of four lines, each with its own new rhymes, and then a final rhyming couplet. When Shakespeare's sonnets were published in 1609, there were a hundred and fifty-four of them, almost all in this form. So where's the turn in the English sonnet? Usually it's delayed until the couplet, which often delivers a sharp twist or summary. That's the standard contrast. But don't apply it too rigidly. Many of Shakespeare's sonnets also shift direction at line nine, just as Petrarch's do. So in practice, the English form often contains two turns, not one.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about literature.
talk: Welcome back. Today: how money shaped the Victorian novel. In the 1830s, a new novel in Britain was usually published in three volumes, and it was very expensive, about a guinea and a half, more than many workers earned in a week. So most readers didn't buy novels. They borrowed them from circulating libraries that charged an annual subscription. Then, in 1836, a young writer named Charles Dickens began publishing The Pickwick Papers in monthly installments. Each part had thirty-two pages and two illustrations, and it cost one shilling. So readers paid a little each month, for about a year and a half. At first, sales were weak; the first part sold only a few hundred copies. But in the fourth installment, Dickens introduced a witty servant named Sam Weller, and sales took off. By the end, each part was selling around forty thousand copies. Now, think about what this format did to writing. A three-volume novel was finished before readers saw it. A serial wasn't. Dickens was often writing just a few weeks ahead of publication, so he could watch sales and readers' letters and adjust his plots. And each installment needed a reason to buy the next one, which encouraged cliffhangers. For a long time, critics treated these features as flaws, saying serial novels were baggy and padded because authors were paid by length. More recently, scholars have argued nearly the opposite: that serialization created a shared, ongoing experience, much like a television series today.

intro: Listen to a talk in a linguistics class.
talk: Here's a pattern you can test yourself. Latin pater, English father. Latin tres, English three. Latin cornu, English horn. Where Latin has a p, English has an f. Where Latin has a t, English has a th. And where Latin has a k sound, English has an h. These aren't random. In 1822, Jacob Grimm, yes, one of the brothers who collected fairy tales, laid out these correspondences systematically, building on work by the Danish scholar Rasmus Rask. Today we call it Grimm's Law. The idea is that the Germanic languages, including English, German, and Dutch, went through a sound shift that Latin and Greek didn't. One set of consonants, p, t, and k, became f, th, and h. Another set, b, d, and g, became p, t, and k. That's why Latin decem corresponds to English ten. Now, linguists think the order mattered. If b, d, and g had become p, t, and k first, those new sounds would have been swept up into the change to f, th, and h. Since they weren't, the first shift probably happened earlier. But Grimm's Law had exceptions. Latin pater should give Gothic a word with th, but Gothic has fadar, with a d. Scholars treated such cases as irregular. Then, in 1875, Karl Verner showed that these exceptions depended on where the stress fell in the original word. The exceptions followed a rule too. And that discovery encouraged a bold claim: that sound changes operate without exceptions.

intro: Listen to a talk in a linguistics class.
talk: A language with no native speakers is usually considered dead. So here's a remarkable case. Hebrew stopped being anyone's everyday spoken language around the second or third century CE. For more than fifteen hundred years after that, it survived, but only in prayer, scholarship, and writing, a bit like Latin in medieval Europe. Then, in 1881, a young man named Eliezer Ben-Yehuda moved to Jerusalem, determined to revive it as a spoken language. He insisted that his family speak only Hebrew at home, and his son, born in 1882, is often called the first native speaker of Hebrew in modern times. He also began a huge dictionary, coining words for modern things. That's the popular story: a single determined man. But historians of language now give much more credit to schools. In the farming settlements of the late 1800s, teachers began teaching all subjects in Hebrew, and children who learned it at school spoke it with each other, and later with their own children. So the revival really happened in three steps: first an ideology, then the classroom, then the homes of the next generation. Compare this with Irish. After Irish independence in 1922, Irish became an official language and was required in schools. Yet today, relatively few use it as their main daily language. One reason: in Palestine, immigrants arrived speaking many different languages, so Hebrew filled a real need as a common language. In Ireland, nearly everyone already shared English.

intro: Listen to a talk in a philosophy class.
talk: In 1967, the British philosopher Philippa Foot published a brief thought experiment. A runaway tram is heading toward five workers on the track. The driver can steer onto a side track, where only one worker stands. Should he? Most people say yes. But Foot paired it with a second case. A judge can stop a deadly riot by framing and executing an innocent man. Again, one life against several, yet almost everyone says no. So what's the difference? Foot drew on distinctions between doing and allowing, and between intending and merely foreseeing. Later, in 1976 and again in 1985, the American philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson pushed the puzzle further and gave it its name, the trolley problem. She introduced two famous variants. In the first, you're a bystander next to a switch, not the driver. In the second, you're on a footbridge above the track, and the only way to stop the trolley is to push a large man off the bridge onto the rails. Surveys consistently show that most people would pull the switch but would not push the man, though the numbers are identical. A common explanation is that pushing uses the man as a means, while switching merely foresees a death as a side effect. But here's a twist. In 2008, Thomson changed her mind. She argued that the bystander, unlike the driver, isn't permitted to switch either, because he'd be imposing a cost on someone else that he wouldn't accept himself.

intro: Listen to a talk in a philosophy class.
talk: Here's a belief you hold with complete confidence: the sun will rise tomorrow. Why? Because it has risen every day so far. That kind of reasoning, from past cases to future ones, is called induction. In 1739, the Scottish philosopher David Hume asked a devastating question: what justifies it? Hume's argument works in two steps. Induction assumes that the future will resemble the past, that nature is uniform. So, step one: can we prove that assumption by pure logic? No. There's no contradiction in imagining that tomorrow the sun doesn't rise. It would be surprising, but it isn't logically impossible, the way a square circle is. Step two: can we prove it from experience? We could say the future has always resembled the past before. But that's itself an inductive argument. We'd be using induction to justify induction, which is circular. So Hume concluded that our expectations rest not on reason but on custom, or habit. After seeing one thing follow another many times, the mind simply expects it. Bertrand Russell later made the point vividly with a chicken. Fed every day, it confidently expects food, until the day the farmer wrings its neck instead. In the twentieth century, Karl Popper accepted Hume's argument but denied that science needs induction at all. Scientists, he said, don't prove theories from repeated observations; they propose bold theories and try to refute them. No number of fed days proves a theory, but one wrung neck can disprove it.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about philosophy.
talk: Welcome back. Today's question: is there anything you can know with absolute certainty? In his 1641 Meditations on First Philosophy, René Descartes tried to answer this by doubting everything he possibly could. His strategy was like sorting a basket of apples: if you suspect some are rotten, you dump them all out and put back only the ones you're sure are good. He doubted in three stages, each stronger than the last. Stage one: the senses. They sometimes deceive us; a tower that looks round from far away turns out to be square up close. But surely I know I'm sitting by the fire, holding this paper? Which leads to stage two: dreaming. He has often dreamed exactly that, and there's no sure sign to tell dreaming from waking. Still, even in dreams, two plus three equals five. So, stage three: suppose there's an evil demon, as powerful as it is deceptive, fooling me even about mathematics. Now, what survives? Descartes noticed that even if he's being deceived, he must exist in order to be deceived. Whenever he thinks 'I am, I exist,' it must be true. The famous version, 'I think, therefore I am,' actually comes from an earlier book, his Discourse on Method, published in 1637. But was even that certain? The eighteenth-century German writer Georg Lichtenberg objected that Descartes was only entitled to say 'there is thinking,' the way we say 'it is raining.' The 'I' itself, Lichtenberg suggested, was an assumption sneaking in.

intro: Listen to a talk in a psychology class.
talk: Before the 1880s, most people assumed memory was too complex to measure scientifically. Then a German psychologist, Hermann Ebbinghaus, decided to try, using the only subject he had complete access to: himself. His key problem was that real words come with associations. If you learn the word 'apple,' it connects to everything you already know. So he invented over two thousand nonsense syllables, things like 'dax' or 'bok,' consonant, vowel, consonant, with no meaning at all. Then he memorized lists of them perfectly and tested himself after different delays. He didn't just ask, how many can I recall? He measured savings: how much less time it took to relearn the list compared with the first time. Even if you can't recall a single item, relearning might be faster, which shows something remained. His 1885 results produced what's called the forgetting curve. The drop is steep at first. Within about an hour, more than half the savings were gone. After a day, about two thirds. But then the curve flattens, so that a month later, he still retained around a fifth. He also found that spreading practice over several days was more efficient than cramming it into one session. Now, compare nonsense syllables with meaningful material. Ebbinghaus also memorized stanzas of a poem by Byron, and those took roughly a tenth of the effort. That points to a real limitation. The very thing that made his method precise, removing meaning, also made it unlike most real-world memory.

intro: Listen to a talk in a psychology class.
talk: In 1932, the British psychologist Frederic Bartlett published a book called Remembering, taking a different approach from earlier memory research, which often used meaningless material to keep things controlled. Bartlett thought that missed the point. Real memory, he argued, is all about meaning. So he gave his participants, students at Cambridge, a Native American folk tale called 'The War of the Ghosts.' To a British reader, it's a strange story: two young men hunting seals hear war cries, join a war party in canoes, and one realizes his companions are ghosts. Bartlett used two methods. In repeated reproduction, the same person retold the story several times, after delays of minutes, months, even years. In serial reproduction, one person's version was passed to a second person, who retold it to a third, a bit like the children's game of telephone. Both methods produced the same kinds of changes. The story got shorter. Unfamiliar details were replaced with familiar ones: canoes became boats, and hunting seals became fishing. And the supernatural element, the ghosts, was often explained away or forgotten. Bartlett explained this with the concept of a schema, organized knowledge that shapes how we take in and recall information. We don't replay memories like a recording; we rebuild them using what we already expect. Now, a caveat. His instructions were informal, and some later researchers who asked participants to be as accurate as possible found fewer distortions. Still, his central claim, that remembering is reconstruction, is now widely accepted.

intro: Listen to a talk in a sociology class.
talk: Suicide seems like the most individual act imaginable. That's exactly why the French sociologist Émile Durkheim chose to study it. In his 1897 book, Suicide, he wanted to show that even this decision has social causes. He compared official statistics across countries and groups and found stable patterns. Suicide rates were higher among Protestants than Catholics, higher among unmarried people than married people, and, interestingly, they fell during wars and political crises. Individual psychology couldn't explain why whole groups differed so consistently, year after year. So Durkheim proposed two social forces. The first is integration, how strongly people are bound into a group. Too little integration produces what he called egoistic suicide. Protestantism, he argued, encouraged individual judgment and integrated people less than Catholicism. Too much integration, where the individual barely matters compared with the group, produces altruistic suicide, like a soldier sacrificing himself. The second force is regulation, how much society limits people's desires. Too little produces anomic suicide, from the word anomie, meaning normlessness. Strikingly, rates rose not only during economic crashes but also during sudden booms. Any rapid change loosens the rules that tell people what to expect. Too much regulation produces fatalistic suicide, which he barely discussed. Critics later raised a problem. Official statistics depend on who records a death as suicide. Where suicide carried strong religious stigma, as in many Catholic areas, families and officials may have reported fewer cases. So some of Durkheim's patterns may partly reflect recording, not reality.

intro: Listen to a talk in an economics class.
talk: In 1857, a German statistician named Ernst Engel studied the household budgets of about two hundred working-class families in Belgium. He noticed a regularity that's now called Engel's law: as a family's income rises, the share of income spent on food falls. Not the amount, the share. Richer families do spend more on food in total, but it takes a smaller fraction of their budget. The poorest families in his data spent around sixty to seventy percent of their income on food. It's one of the most reliable patterns in economics, holding across countries and time. In fact, it became a standard way to compare living standards. If you want to know how well-off a population is, look at its food share. Here's a famous application. In the early 1960s, an American economist named Mollie Orshansky needed a way to define poverty. She knew from a 1955 survey that a typical family spent about one third of its income on food. So she took the cost of a minimal food budget and multiplied it by three. That became the basis of the official US poverty line. But notice what Engel's law implies. As the country grew richer, the food share kept falling, well below one third. Yet the poverty line was mainly updated for inflation, not rebuilt from new spending patterns. So many economists argue that the multiplier of three is outdated, since housing, health care, and childcare now take a much bigger share of family budgets.

options: A pattern in food spending and how it was used to measure poverty

questions.explanation: Because the food share kept falling as incomes rose, she says many economists consider the multiplier outdated.

intro: Listen to a talk in an economics class.
talk: In 1958, a New Zealand-born economist working in London, A. W. Phillips, published a study of British data covering nearly a century, from 1861 to 1957. He found a strikingly consistent relationship: when unemployment was low, wages rose quickly, and when unemployment was high, wages rose slowly or even fell. In 1960, the American economists Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow restated the idea in terms of prices. Plotting US data, they suggested a tradeoff between inflation and unemployment. Policymakers loved this, because it looked like a menu. Want lower unemployment? Accept a bit more inflation. Then, in 1968, Milton Friedman argued that the menu was an illusion, at least in the long run. His reasoning went in stages. Suppose the government stimulates the economy and inflation rises. At first, workers don't expect the higher inflation, so they accept wage offers that look generous, and unemployment falls. But in the second stage, workers notice that prices have risen, and they start demanding higher wages to keep up. Firms hire less, and unemployment drifts back to what Friedman called its natural rate. Now the economy has the same unemployment as before, but higher inflation. The 1970s seemed to confirm this. Many Western economies suffered high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, so-called stagflation, which the simple curve said shouldn't happen. Today, economists still use a Phillips curve, but one in which expectations play a central role. The tradeoff exists, but only temporarily.

questions.explanation: High inflation with high unemployment contradicted the simple curve and seemed to confirm Friedman's argument.

intro: Listen to a talk in a business class.
talk: In January 1914, the Ford Motor Company announced something that stunned American industry: it would pay workers five dollars a day. At the time, Ford's typical wage was about two dollars and thirty-four cents for a nine-hour day, so this roughly doubled pay, and it cut the workday to eight hours. Why? Let's go back one year. In 1913, Ford introduced the moving assembly line at its Highland Park plant. Productivity soared. But the work was monotonous and exhausting, and workers quit in huge numbers. Turnover that year reached about three hundred seventy percent. In other words, to keep a workforce of around fourteen thousand people, the company had to hire more than fifty thousand over the year. Every new worker had to be trained, and every departure slowed the line. So the five-dollar day was a business decision. And it worked. After it was introduced, turnover dropped dramatically and absenteeism fell. Henry Ford later called it one of the finest cost-cutting moves the company ever made. Economists call this an efficiency wage: paying above the market rate because it raises productivity. Now, there's a popular story that Ford raised wages so workers could afford to buy Ford cars. That might have been a small bonus, but most historians doubt it was the main reason. Ford's own workers were a tiny fraction of its customers. And there was a catch. To qualify, workers had to meet standards of personal behavior, checked by company investigators who visited their homes.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about business.
talk: Today: how Toyota changed the way factories think about inventory. After World War Two, American companies like Ford relied on mass production: make huge numbers of identical parts, store them in warehouses, and push them down the line, just in case they're needed. That requires lots of space and lots of capital, and Toyota had neither. An engineer named Taiichi Ohno, working from the late 1940s on, came up with an alternative. His inspiration, reportedly, was the American supermarket. In a supermarket, shelves aren't filled based on a forecast. A customer takes a can of soup, and only then does the store restock that can. So Ohno reversed the flow. Instead of pushing parts forward, each step pulls parts from the step before, only when needed. The signal was a simple card called a kanban. When a box of parts was used up, its card went back to the previous process, ordering exactly that many more. This became known as just-in-time production. A second idea was even older. In the 1920s, Sakichi Toyoda, the father of Toyota's founder, had invented a loom that stopped automatically when a thread broke. Ohno extended this: any worker could stop the entire line on spotting a defect. That sounds wasteful, but it meant problems were fixed immediately, not built into hundreds of cars. Now, just-in-time has a weakness. With almost no inventory, a single disruption can halt production. After the 2011 earthquake in Japan, Toyota itself began keeping larger stockpiles of critical parts.

intro: Listen to a talk in an education class.
talk: Today: Maria Montessori, whose methods are still used worldwide. She didn't start as a teacher. In 1896, she became one of the first women in Italy to earn a medical degree, and her early work was with children who had intellectual disabilities. With carefully designed materials, these children learned far more than expected, which made her wonder about other children. Her chance came on January sixth, 1907, when she opened the Casa dei Bambini, the Children's House, in a poor district of Rome called San Lorenzo. The children came from working families in a new housing project. So what made her classroom different? Picture a typical school of the time: rows of fixed desks, a teacher at the front, every child doing the same task at the same moment. Montessori's room had child-sized tables and chairs that children could move. Children of different ages worked together, and they chose their own activities from shelves of materials. Many materials were self-correcting. For example, a wooden block with holes for cylinders of different sizes: if a child puts a cylinder in the wrong hole, one will be left over, so the child discovers the error without an adult. The teacher's job was mainly to observe and guide. Her ideas spread quickly to the United States around 1912, then collapsed. In 1914, the American educator William Kilpatrick published a critique calling her methods outdated and too narrow, and interest faded for decades. Not until the late 1950s did American Montessori schools return.

intro: Listen to a talk in an education class.
talk: If you've taken a teacher-training course, you've probably seen a colorful pyramid labeled Bloom's taxonomy. But its real story is different from the pyramid. In 1956, a team led by the educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom published a framework that classified learning goals into six levels. From bottom to top: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. The idea was that each level builds on the ones below it. You can't analyze something you don't comprehend. Now, here's the part people forget. The original purpose wasn't to guide teaching at all. It was to help university examiners. Examiners at different universities wanted to share test questions, and needed a common vocabulary for what each question measured. And the original handbook had no pyramid; that came later. Then, in 2001, a group including several of Bloom's former students and colleagues published a revision. They made two important changes. First, they turned the nouns into verbs: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create. That emphasized what learners actually do. Second, they swapped the top two levels. Synthesis, now renamed create, moved to the very top, above evaluate. Their reasoning was that producing something new is generally more demanding than judging something that already exists. Some educators have questioned the hierarchy itself, though. The pyramid makes remembering look like the least important level. But you can't evaluate an argument about history without knowing a good deal of history. So critics argue that the lower levels aren't less valuable, just more basic.

intro: Listen to a talk in a media studies class.
talk: On the evening of October 30, 1938, the night before Halloween, CBS radio broadcast an adaptation of H. G. Wells's novel The War of the Worlds, produced by Orson Welles and his Mercury Theatre company. The clever twist was the format. Instead of simply narrating the story, the first part was presented as a series of news bulletins interrupting a music program: reports of explosions on Mars, then a strange object landing at a farm in Grovers Mill, New Jersey, then creatures emerging and attacking. The next morning, newspapers across the country carried headlines about mass panic: people fleeing their homes, jamming phone lines, crowding the roads. And in 1940, a Princeton researcher named Hadley Cantril published a study estimating that about six million people had heard the broadcast and more than a million had been frightened. For decades, it served as the classic example of media power. More recent historians have looked again, and the picture has changed. First, the audience was small. A ratings survey that night found only about two percent of respondents listening to the program; most people were tuned to a popular comedy show on another network. Second, the newspaper reports were mostly based on anecdotes, and many were quickly exaggerated. Why? Radio was their fast-growing competitor for advertising money, and a story about radio's irresponsibility served their interests. So, some people were frightened, certainly. But the mass panic was, to a large extent, a media creation itself, just not by radio.

intro: Listen to a talk in a media studies class.
talk: In New York in the early 1830s, a daily newspaper usually meant a mercantile paper, full of shipping news, commodity prices, and political speeches. It cost six cents a copy, but usually you couldn't buy single copies; you paid an annual subscription of around ten dollars, more than many workers earned in a week. These papers were aimed at merchants and politicians, and many survived on support from political parties. Then, on September 3, 1833, a young printer named Benjamin Day launched the New York Sun, priced at one penny. Day changed three things at once. First, distribution: instead of subscriptions, boys sold the paper on street corners, one copy at a time. Second, content: instead of shipping lists, the Sun ran crime reports, stories from the police court, and human-interest tales about ordinary people. And third, the business model. At one cent, the paper couldn't make money from sales alone. Profit came from advertisers paying to reach a huge audience. Within a few years, the Sun had one of the largest circulations in the world. In 1835, it even ran articles claiming a famous astronomer had found creatures on the Moon, and sales jumped. So how should we judge the penny press? Historians used to see it mainly as the birth of sensationalism, and the Moon story supports that. But many now emphasize something else: by depending on advertisers and readers rather than parties, newspapers became more independent of politics, and news became something meant for everyone.
